papers.title_in_file: Ultra-efﬁcient and highly-tunable second-harmonic generation in Z-cut periodically poled lithium niobate nanowaveguides
papers.version_note: arXiv:2004.02056v1 preprint, compiled April 7, 2020; the text layer holds one copy.
papers.what_it_is: A Letter that combines group velocity engineering with periodic poling in a Z-cut thin-film lithium niobate waveguide to get both high second-harmonic efficiency and large, blue-shifting thermal tunability.

assertions.value: The authors report second-harmonic generation in a millimeter-long Z-cut LNOI waveguide at 1900 ± 500%W−1cm−2 efficiency and with a tunability of -1.71 nm/K from 1530 to 1583 nm, by type-0 quasi-phase-matching.
quotes: On a millimeter-long, Zcut LNOI waveguide, we demonstrate ultra-efﬁcient (1900 ± 500%W−1cm−2)
and highly tunable (-1.71 nm/K) second-harmonic generation from 1530 to 1583 nm by type-0 quasi-phase-matching
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one device in one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper does not state how the efficiency is normalized or whether coupling loss is removed; the 1900 figure is the mean over the tuning range and 2400 is the peak, as the text reads.

assertions.value: The authors report that the highest measured efficiency is up to 2400 % W−1cm−2, with a phase matching bandwidth of about 18 nm.

assertions.value: The authors report that the phase matching blue shifts with increasing temperature at a linear rate of 1.71 nm/K, measured from 25◦C to 55◦C at 5 ◦C steps.
quotes: linear rate of 1.71 nm/K.
Measured phase matching curves of the LNOI waveguide blue shifted as the temperature increases from 25◦C to 55◦C at 5 ◦C step.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one device.

assertions.value: The authors report that the measured tunability (∼ 1.71 nm/K) is almost 3 times larger than the simulated result (∼ 0.6 nm/K).
quotes: We notice that the measured tunability (∼ 1.71 nm/K) is almost 3 times larger than the simulated result (∼ 0.6 nm/K), as shown in Figure. 5(b).
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical comparison of one device against one simulation.
assertions.reader_inference: The simulated value of 0.6 nm/K is for Waveguide 2 at 700×1500 nm; the fabricated device is described as that configuration, but its simulation is not rerun on measured dimensions.

assertions.value: The authors state that the waveguide also experiences effects such as thermal expansion and pyroelectric effect that the current model does not consider, and that they leave their investigation to future work; they do not show that these effects explain the gap.
quotes: In addition to the thermo-optic effect, the waveguide also experiences various other effects, such as the thermal expansion and pyroelectric effect, which are not considering in the current model.
We will need to investigate in our future work.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the limit of its own model in Section 2.

assertions.value: The authors report excellent consistency from 1530 to 1583 nm with ± 500% variation in efficiency, which they attribute mainly to coupling instability, and a bandwidth that varies within ± 1.5 nm due to material inhomogeneity or imperfect poling.
quotes: Figure 5(a) also shows excellent consistency from 1530 to 1583
nm with ± 500% variation in efﬁciency, attributed mainly to the coupling instability.
Meanwhile, the bandwidth varies within ± 1.5 nm due to material inhomogeneity or imperfect poling.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result; the attribution of causes is the authors' own statement.
assertions.reader_inference: The 500 figure in the headline is therefore a spread across the tuning range that the authors assign to coupling, not a statistical error bar.

assertions.value: The authors state that the PPLN waveguides are fabricated on a Z-cut LNOI wafer with a 700 nm thick LN thin film bonded on a 2-µm thermally grown silicon dioxide layer, shallow-etched by ion milling to about 480 nm, and covered with a 2 µm silicon oxide overclad by PECVD.
quotes: which is a 700 nm thick LN thin ﬁlm bonded on a 2-µm thermally grown silicon dioxide layer above a silicon substrate
an optimized ion milling process is used to shallowly etch the waveguide structure (∼ 480 nm)
we apply an overclad layer of 2 µm silicon oxide on the chip with via Plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition (PECVD)
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own fabrication in Section 1.B.

assertions.value: The authors state that the poling electrodes are 30-nm Cr and 60-nm Au layers, that several 1-ms high voltage (∼550 V) electrical pulses form the domain inversion, and that the whole sample is held on a heater at about 300◦C, which they call a critical factor in reducing the required voltage.
quotes: Then 30-nm Cr and 60-nm Au layers are deposited via electron-beam evaporation
We apply several 1-ms high voltage (∼550 V) electrical pulses on the poling pads to form the domain inversion region.
The whole sample is placed on high temperature (∼ 300◦C) heater.
Elevated temperature is a critical factor in order to reduce the required corrective voltage for thin-ﬁlm lithium niobate.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own poling process in Section 1.B.

assertions.value: The authors report, from SEM images after HF etching, uniform periodic domain inversion along the propagation direction with a 3.8 µm poling period, and good poling uniformity in thickness down to 480 nm in depth, which they say is quite challenging for thick (> 400 nm) lithium niobate.
quotes: we obtain uniform periodic domain inversion along light propagation direction with such short poling period 3.8 µm.
we achieve good poling uniformity in thickness (down to 480 nm in depth), which is quite challenging for thick (> 400 nm) lithium niobate.
assertions.certainty_reason: A qualitative empirical result from SEM imaging of one device.
assertions.reader_inference: No quantitative uniformity metric or yield is given.

assertions.value: The authors derive, by Taylor expansion of the quasi-phase-matching condition with the poling period held fixed, that the temperature tuning rate of the fundamental frequency equals the difference of the second-harmonic and fundamental thermo-optic coefficients multiplied by the group velocity mismatch and the speed of light over the fundamental angular frequency, so the group velocity mismatch sets both the magnitude and the direction of the shift.
quotes: with the same poling period
pansion is neglected here)
Hence, GVM can serve as an efﬁcient knob to control the tunability, both for its magnitude and the direction of the QPM wavelength shifting.
assertions.certainty_reason: A derivation in Section 1.A; the equation itself is lost in the text layer, so the value is held to the quoted sentences and the conditions (fixed period, thermal expansion neglected) are quoted.
assertions.reader_inference: The equation text is split across lines in the layer; the reading of Eq. (4) comes from the displayed terms, not a quote.

assertions.value: The authors state that they simulate optical modes and their temperature dependency in Lumerical MODE with a temperature-dependent Sellmeier equation, for two LNOI geometries (Waveguide 1: 400×1850 nm and Waveguide 2: 700×1500 nm) using fundamental quasi-TM modes at the fundamental and second-harmonic wavelengths, with a simulated sidewall angle of 62◦, and calculated type-0 poling periods of 2.45 µm and 3.8 µm respectively.
quotes: We validate the theoretical prediction through performing MODE simulations of optical modes and their temperature dependency (Lumerical, Inc).
(Waveguide 1: 400×1850 nm and Waveguide 2: 700×1500 nm)
the poling period for type-0 phase matching is calculated to be 2.45 µm and 3.8 µm, respectively.
The simulated sidewall angle in is 62◦ for all ﬁgures.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own simulation setup in Section 1.A and Fig. 1.

assertions.value: The authors report from simulation that Waveguide 1 red shifts at a 0.2 nm/K slope while Waveguide 2 blue shifts at a 0.6 nm/K slope, and from these numbers extract group velocity mismatch of -600 fs/mm and 180 fs/mm respectively.
quotes: Waveguide 1 exhibits red shift with a 0.2 nm/K slope. However, Waveguide 2 exhibits blue shifting with 0.6 nm/K slope
From these numbers we extract their GVM to be -600 fs/mm and 180 fs/mm, respectively.
assertions.certainty_reason: A simulation result from one model.
assertions.reader_inference: The GVM values are back-computed from the simulated slopes, so agreement between them and the slopes is not an independent check.

assertions.value: The authors state that the ratio of the absolute values of the two group velocity mismatches reveals the ratio of the thermal tunabilities, and that the simulation results are in good agreement with their theoretical prediction.
quotes: Also the ratio of the absolute value of their GVMs reveals the ratio of amplitude of corresponding thermal tunability.
The above simulation results are in good agreement with our theoretical prediction, validating the relationship between GVM and thermal tunability.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim; the check compares quantities extracted from the same simulation.
assertions.reader_inference: Ratio of absolute GVM is 600 to 180, about 3.3, and ratio of slopes is 0.2 to 0.6 inverted, about 3; the paper does not show this arithmetic.

assertions.value: The authors state that a thicker lithium niobate layer (∼700 nm) gives a small and positive GVM (<200 fs/mm) and so larger thermal tunability, and that for 700×1500 nm the required poling period is 55% larger than for the thinner waveguide.
quotes: By using a thicker layer of lithium niobate (∼700 nm), we are able to achieve small and positive GVM (<200 fs/mm) to obtain larger thermal tunability.
With the waveguide geometry of 700×1500 nm, the required poling period is 55% larger than the thinner one
assertions.certainty_reason: A simulation-based design statement.

assertions.value: The authors state that their approach first minimizes the group velocity mismatch between the interacting wavelengths and then uses periodic poling to compensate the phase mismatch, which they say sustains high conversion efficiency using d33 while enhancing the QPM tunability.
quotes: we ﬁrst minimize the group velocity mismatch (GVM) between the interacting wavelengths and then use appropriate periodic poling to compensate for their phase mismatching.
It is this two-step optimization that gives rise to the high efﬁciency and large tunability at the same time.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's description of the approach and its credit for the result.

assertions.value: The authors state that the technique is not reproducible in bulky PPLN waveguides because their modal dispersion is dominated by material dispersion owing to a much larger cross section (e.g., >3×3 µm), which prohibits the group velocity maneuvering.
quotes: It is also not reproducible in bulky PPLN waveguides [13, 14], whose modal dispersion is dominated by the material dispersion due to a much larger cross section (e.g., >3×3 µm)
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the scope of its own method in the Introduction.

assertions.value: The authors state that a type-I scheme gets high tunability but takes a 30-fold reduction in SHG efficiency because it uses d31, typically 4.7 pm/V against about 27 pm/V for d33, while type-0 quasi-phase matching uses d33 for high efficiency but suffers a lower tunability, an unfavorable trade-off.
quotes: However, such a scheme takes on a 30-fold reduction in the SHG efﬁciency, as it uses LNOI’s d31 nonlinear susceptibility whose
typical value of 4.7 pm/V is much lower than that of d33 at ∼27 pm/V.
This unfavorable trade-off between the efﬁciency and tunability poses a limitation in achieving higher performance of nonlinear optical devices made of lithium-niobate.
assertions.certainty_reason: A characterization of prior work (the paper's references 5, 13, 14) with typical values.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper also says the type-I efficiency loss is over 30 times in Section 1.A, p.2.

assertions.value: The authors state that the QPM wavelength uniquely blue shifts at a large tunability as temperature rises, that the phase matching profiles remain in a near-ideal sinc squared shape with high peak efficiency over the tuning range, and, to the best of their knowledge, that this blue shifting is distinct from bulky LN or other LNOI waveguides reported so far.
quotes: Uniquely, the QPM wavelength exhibits blue shifts at a large tunability as the temperature is increased.
the phase matching proﬁles remain in a near-ideal sinc2 shape and maintain high peak conversion efﬁciency over the entirely tuning range.
To the best of our knowledge, such blue
is quite distinct to bulky LN waveguides or
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's novelty claim, stated to the best of their knowledge.

assertions.value: The authors state that the tuning range is currently limited only by the external temperature controller, which could be replaced by an on-chip microheater to give an even larger tuning range; this is not shown.
quotes: Currently, the tuning range is limited only by the external temperature controller, which can be replaced by an on-chip microheater [19] to provide an even larger tuning range.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim without a measurement.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that the tunability is obtained without degrading conversion efficiency or bandwidth, that it is valuable for offsetting nanofabrication errors of χ(2) circuits integrated in mass on chip, and that about 18 nm broadband phase matching is maintained in well maintained profiles over 50 nm of thermal tuning.
quotes: This exceptional tunability, obtained without degrading the conversion efﬁciency or bandwidth, is valuable in offsetting inevitable nanofabrication errors of χ(2) circuits
with broadband (about 18 nm) phase matching in well maintained proﬁles over 50 nm of thermal tuning
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' conclusion, with no comparison against a non-engineered device in this paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The 'without degrading' claim is made against prior LNOI work by argument, not by a side-by-side measurement; the efficiency varies by ± 500% across the range.

assertions.value: The authors state that the technique is applicable to quantum light sources and other photonic information processing across visible to mid-IR bands, and that type-0 periodic poling could potentially be applied to LNOI microring cavities for much higher conversion efficiency towards single photon nonlinearity; neither is demonstrated.
quotes: Our technique is applicable to optical harmonic generation, quantum light sources, frequency conversion, and many other photonic information processing across visible to mid-IR spectral bands.
could potentially be applied to LNOI microring cavities for signiﬁcantly enhanced frequency conversion efﬁciency towards single photon nonlinearity
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's outlook without evidence in this paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper's own experiments are classical continuous-wave SHG; no quantum light source is built or measured here.
